title: Teacher Told My Daughter With Down Syndrome Face Paint "Wouldn't Make Her Pretty," So I Walked Straight Up to Her Table
fb_text:
My 6-Year-Old Came Home Crying From Her First School Party Because Her Teacher Said Face Paint Wouldn't Make Her Pretty

My daughter had been looking forward to her very first school party for weeks. But barely an hour after I dropped her off, the principal called to tell me she was crying and desperately asking for me. When I got there, my little girl told me that her new teacher had refused to paint her face like the other children, saying, "Makeup doesn't make little girls like you pretty."

My daughter, Victoria, is six years old, and she has Down syndrome.

Enrolling her in first grade was one of the hardest decisions I have ever made as a mother.

I worried constantly. Would the other children accept her? Would they tease her? Would she understand if someone was unkind? And most of all, would she feel safe enough to tell me if something hurt her?

But Victoria was determined to go. She had dreamed of it for so long, and during those first two weeks I had never seen her so happy. Every afternoon she threw herself into my arms and told me all about her new friends, her little adventures and the colorful drawings she had made that day.

Then came the day of her first school party.

I kissed her forehead, helped her with her things and dropped her off. Everything seemed fine.

Until my phone rang less than an hour later. It was the principal.

"Mrs. Parker, Victoria has been crying for quite a while. She keeps asking us to call you. Could you come to the school?"

"What happened? Is she hurt?"

"Physically she's fine, but she's extremely upset."

I didn't ask anything else. I grabbed my keys and rushed out.

When I arrived, I found Victoria in the hallway, surrounded by children running around happily, their faces painted in a hundred colors. Some had butterflies on their cheeks, others flowers or tiny stars.

Not far away, a young teacher was carefully painting a design on another little girl's face. The moment Victoria saw me, she ran over and buried herself in my arms.

"Mom, I don't want to stay here anymore. I want to go home."

I gently held her shoulders and looked into her tear-filled eyes.

"Sweetheart, can you tell me what happened?"

She pointed at the teacher, who was busy with another child and hadn't noticed us.

"She told me face paint is only for pretty girls. She said it wouldn't make me pretty, because I'm not."

My heart sank.

I crouched down so I could look my daughter straight in the eyes.

"Mom, am I ugly? Will I never be pretty? Tell me the truth, please."

I wiped the tears from her cheeks, kissed her forehead and held her tight.

"Victoria, listen to me. You are beautiful in every way. Never, ever believe anyone who tells you otherwise."

She looked at me with those innocent eyes.

"But Mom, she's a teacher. Teachers are supposed to tell the truth, right?"

For a moment, I had no words.

I glanced at the woman. She was laughing with another child, happily carrying on with her face painting, completely unaware of the harm her words had done to my daughter.

Suddenly, an idea came to me.

I took Victoria's hands gently.

"Sweetheart, why don't you go back to the principal's office? Tell her Mom will be there in five minutes. I just have one little thing to take care of first."

"Are we going home now?"

"We're going to the movies, my love. And then we'll get your favorite ice cream. You deserve a wonderful afternoon. I promise."

Victoria hugged me one last time and headed back down the hallway.

I watched until she disappeared into the principal's office.

Then I slowly turned to the teacher.

She had never seen me before. She had no idea who I was, or that the little girl she had just humiliated was my daughter.

And I decided not to reveal that just yet.

Because no child should ever have to question her own beauty or her own worth because of an adult's thoughtless words.

This teacher was about to learn something she clearly had not understood.

So I walked straight to her table, just as she was finishing painting another little girl's face…

When I arrived, Victoria told me her new teacher had refused to paint her face like the other children. The teacher had said, "Makeup doesn't make little girls like you pretty."

A Hard Decision

Enrolling her in first grade was one of the most difficult choices I have ever made as a mother. I worried constantly. Would the other children accept her? Would they laugh at her? Would she understand if someone was unkind? And above all, would she feel safe enough to tell me if something hurt her?

The Phone Call

Then the day of the school party arrived. I kissed her forehead, helped her with her things and dropped her off. Everything seemed perfect.

Less than an hour later, my phone rang. It was the principal.

"Mrs. Parker, Victoria has been crying for quite a while. She keeps asking us to call you. Could you come to the school?"

"Is she hurt?" I asked.

"Physically she's fine, but she's very upset."

I grabbed my keys and left at once.

What Victoria Said

In the hallway, children ran past with their faces painted in bright colors, butterflies, flowers and tiny stars on their cheeks. A young teacher was carefully painting another little girl's face nearby. The moment Victoria saw me, she ran into my arms.

"Mom, I don't want to stay here. I want to go home."

I held her shoulders and looked into her tearful eyes. "Sweetheart, what happened?"

She pointed at the teacher, who hadn't noticed us. "She said face paint is only for pretty girls. She said it wouldn't make me pretty, because I'm not."

My heart sank. I crouched down to meet her eyes.

"Mom, am I ugly? Will I never be pretty? Tell me the truth, please."

I wiped her tears, kissed her forehead and held her close. "Victoria, listen to me. You are beautiful in every way. Never, ever believe anyone who tells you otherwise."

"But Mom, she's a teacher," she whispered. "Teachers are supposed to tell the truth, right?"

For a moment, I couldn't speak.

Facing the Teacher

The teacher was laughing with another child, completely unaware of the damage she had done. I asked Victoria to go wait in the principal's office and told her I'd be there in five minutes.

"Are we going home?"

"We're going to the movies, my love. Then we'll get your favorite ice cream. You deserve a wonderful afternoon. I promise."

She hugged me and walked down the hall. I watched until she disappeared through the office door.

Then I turned to the teacher. She had never met me. She had no idea the child she had humiliated was my daughter. I chose not to say so yet, because no child should have to doubt her beauty or her worth because of an adult's careless words.

I walked straight to her table as she finished painting another girl's face.

"Excuse me," I said calmly. "I'd like a word."

She smiled politely, until I told her who I was. Her smile faded as I repeated exactly what she had said to Victoria. She tried to explain that it was only a joke, that she hadn't meant anything by it. I told her that a six-year-old doesn't hear jokes from her teacher. She hears the truth.

"My daughter asked me if she was ugly," I said quietly. "Because you told her so."

The teacher's face went pale. She looked down and, for the first time, found no words. I did not raise my voice. I did not need to. The principal had joined us, and she heard everything.

A Better Afternoon

The principal apologized to me sincerely and promised that the matter would be taken seriously. I made it clear that Victoria deserved a teacher who would see her as a child worthy of every colorful butterfly, not one who would decide who was pretty enough.

Then I went to the office, took my daughter's hand and walked her out to the car.

That afternoon, we watched a movie, shared a huge bowl of her favorite ice cream and laughed until her cheeks hurt. At home, I took out my own makeup and painted a small butterfly on her cheek. She stood in front of the mirror for a long time.

"Mom," she said at last, smiling. "I look beautiful."

"You always did, my darling," I told her. "You always did."

Words from an adult can stay with a child for a lifetime. Choose them with kindness, because some children believe every single one.

source.text:
Ma fille attendait avec impatience sa toute première fête à l’école. Mais à peine une heure après que je l’y ai déposée, la directrice m’a appelée pour me dire qu’elle pleurait et qu’elle réclamait désespérément ma présence. À mon arrivée, ma petite fille m’a confié que sa nouvelle institutrice avait refusé de lui maquiller le visage comme aux autres enfants, lui affirmant que « le maquillage ne rend pas jolies les petites filles comme toi ».

Ma fille de six ans, Victoria, est porteuse de trisomie 21.

Décider de l’inscrire au CP a été l’un des choix les plus difficiles que j’aie eu à faire en tant que mère.

Je m’inquiétais constamment. Les autres enfants allaient-ils l’accepter ? Allait-elle subir des moqueries ? Comprendrait-elle si quelqu’un se montrait méchant envers elle ? Et, surtout, se sentirait-elle suffisamment en confiance pour me dire si quelque chose l’avait blessée ?

Mais Victoria était déterminée à aller à l’école. Elle en rêvait depuis si longtemps, et durant ces deux premières semaines, je ne l’avais jamais vue aussi heureuse.

Chaque après-midi, elle se jetait dans mes bras, me racontant avec enthousiasme ses nouveaux camarades, ses petites aventures et les dessins colorés qu’elle avait réalisés au cours de la journée.

Puis est arrivé le jour de sa première fête à l’école.

Je l’ai embrassée sur le front, l’ai aidée avec ses affaires et l’ai déposée à l’école. Tout semblait aller pour le mieux.

Jusqu’à ce que mon téléphone sonne, moins d’une heure plus tard.

C’était la directrice.

« Madame Parker, Victoria pleure depuis un bon moment. Elle ne cesse de nous demander de vous appeler. Pourriez-vous venir à l’école ? »

« Que se passe-t-il ? Est-il arrivé quelque chose ? Est-elle blessée ? »

« Physiquement, elle va bien, mais elle est extrêmement bouleversée. »

Je n’ai posé aucune autre question. J’ai attrapé mes clés et je suis sortie en toute hâte.

À mon arrivée, j’ai trouvé Victoria dans le couloir, entourée d’enfants qui couraient joyeusement, le visage peint de mille couleurs. Certains avaient des papillons dessinés sur les joues, d’autres des fleurs ou de petites étoiles.

Non loin de là, une jeune institutrice peignait minutieusement un motif sur le visage d’une autre petite fille. Dès qu’elle m’a aperçue, Victoria a couru vers moi et s’est blottie dans mes bras.

« Maman, je ne veux plus rester ici. Je veux rentrer à la maison. »

J’ai doucement saisi ses épaules et plongé mon regard dans ses yeux emplis de larmes.

« Ma chérie, peux-tu me dire ce qui s’est passé ? »

Elle a désigné l’institutrice, qui, occupée avec un autre enfant, ne nous avait pas remarquées.

« Elle m’a dit que le maquillage, c’est seulement pour les jolies filles. Elle a dit que ça ne me rendrait pas jolie, parce que je ne le suis pas. »

Mon cœur s’est serré.

Je me suis accroupie pour pouvoir regarder ma fille droit dans les yeux.

« Maman, est-ce que je suis moche ? Est-ce que je ne serai jamais belle ? Dis-moi la vérité, s’il te plaît. »

J’ai essuyé les larmes sur ses joues, déposé un baiser sur son front et l’ai serrée fort contre moi.

« Victoria, écoute-moi bien. Tu es belle, sous tous les rapports. Ne crois jamais, au grand jamais, quelqu’un qui te dit le contraire. »

Elle m’a regardée avec ses yeux pleins d’innocence.

« Mais maman, c’est une institutrice. Les institutrices sont censées dire la vérité, non ? »

Pendant un instant, les mots m’ont manqué.

J’ai jeté un coup d’œil vers la femme. Elle riait avec un autre enfant, poursuivant joyeusement son activité de maquillage, totalement inconsciente du mal que ses paroles avaient causé à ma fille.

Soudain, une idée m’est venue.

J’ai pris délicatement les mains de Victoria.

« Ma chérie, pourquoi ne retournerais-tu pas au bureau de la directrice ? Dis-lui que maman arrive dans cinq minutes. J’ai juste une petite chose à régler avant. »

« On rentre à la maison, maintenant ? »

« On va au cinéma, mon cœur. Et après, on ira manger ta glace préférée. Tu mérites un après-midi merveilleux. Je te le promets. »

Victoria m’a enlacée une dernière fois avant de repartir dans le couloir.

Je l’ai suivie du regard jusqu’à ce qu’elle disparaisse dans le bureau de la directrice.

Puis, je me suis lentement tournée vers l’institutrice.

Elle ne m’avait jamais vue auparavant. Elle n’avait aucune idée de qui j’étais, ni du fait que la petite fille qu’elle venait d’humilier était ma fille.

Et j’ai décidé de ne pas encore révéler la chose.

Car aucun enfant ne devrait jamais avoir à remettre en question sa propre beauté ou sa propre valeur à cause des paroles irréfléchies d’un adulte.

Cette institutrice était sur le point d’apprendre quelque chose qu’elle n’avait manifestement pas compris.

Je me suis donc dirigée droit vers sa table, au moment précis où elle terminait de peindre le visage d’une autre petite fille…

Écrivez « OUI » si vous êtes prêt(e) pour la suite, et je vous l’enverrai sans tarder. 👇👇
